en: Now, as you saw, many comments are bad, but
actually there also are acceptable or good
comments out there.
For example, one kind of comment you will
see in some code files would be legal
information.
Again, this example code file from before,
which contains many bad comments, it also
does have such a legal disclaimer or such a
legal comment right at the top.
And depending on the kind of project you're
working on, you might be required to add
something like this to every code file you
write.
Of course, if it's your own project, you can
decide this on your own if you need that or
not, but in a lot of organizations, you
might be required to add something like
this.
And then of course, it's absolutely fine to
do so.
I mean, you don't really have an alternative
to that anyways.
It doesn't really hurt the code readability
though because it sits right at the top of
the file. It's clear that it contains legal
information and therefore it can easily be
skipped and ignored.
Now another kind of comment which is
actually good is a comment that adds an
explanation which can't be delivered or
replaced by proper naming.
And this would be an example. We're using a
regular expression, and even though that's a
relatively simple one,
regular expressions can get quite long.
And having a little comment next to it which
simply explains what this regular expression
does or checks for can be worth a lot.
Another kind of comment which could make
sense would be a comment that warns you of
something.
For example, here we have a comment warning
us that this specific API, the localStorage
API,
is only available in JavaScript running in
the browser, not running on another machine
with Node.js, for example.
Now, we can always argue whether we really
need this comment. I mean, after all, you
could expect fellow developers to be aware
of that or you might want to place it in a
try-catch block or some if statement
anyways. But if you have neither of that for
some good reason, then adding a warning like
that could make sense.
Now, last but not least, a comment which is
also okay to have would be a to-do note.
You see one here.
Even though that file had a lot of bad
comments, this is not one of the bad
comments. This to-do note can make sense.
Now, of course, we could argue whether we
should have an empty method where everything
is missing and if it wouldn't be better to
just remove it and then add it all in one
go. But if you do have some code which is
unfinished, adding a note like this can
indeed make sense and can be okay.
Of course, you shouldn't overdo it though,
and instead you should focus on writing code
which you finish instead of leaving
unfinished code sitting around in your
codebase.
Now, one last kind of comment which can make
sense is a comment where you add
documentation, especially when providing a
public API. So methods, properties, classes
which can be used by other people, not just
in your organization, but maybe also from
all around the world. If you're building a
library which you wanna share as a
third-party library with other people,
then adding documentation strings which can
be picked up by IDEs, for example, of course
also makes sense.
And here it then really comes down to the
programming language you're using. For
example, for Python, you have a certain
structure for how such documentation strings
should like, and other programming languages
might bring their own conventions.
So documentation comments are a special kind
of comment which can make sense depending on
which kind of project you are working on.
And that is already it for comments.
Hence, the general rule really is that you
should avoid comments with the few
exceptions I showed you over the last
minutes.
